lessons.title: Mixtures, solutions and changes in materials
lessons.programRef: MINEDUB primary school curriculum (English-speaking subsystem), Level III (Class 5) — Elementary Science and Technology; to be checked against the official syllabus
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Say what a mixture and a solution are.
Choose a way of separating a mixture.
Tell physical changes from chemical changes.
reviewNotes: Chemical vs physical change is introduced with everyday examples only.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Mixtures and solutions
blocks.md: A **mixture** has two or more materials together that are not joined chemically (sand and water, rice and stones). A **solution** forms when a **solute** dissolves in a **solvent**: sugar (solute) dissolves in water (solvent) to make a sugar solution. A dissolved solid cannot be seen but is still there: taste the water or let it evaporate.

blocks.caption: Ways of separating mixtures.
blocks.alt: A table of methods: sieving separates big from small pieces; filtering separates solid from liquid; evaporation separates a dissolved solid from a liquid; a magnet separates iron; decanting separates a liquid from a settled solid; each with an example.

blocks.title: Changes
blocks.md: In a **physical change** no new substance is made and it can often be reversed: melting ice, dissolving sugar, cutting paper. In a **chemical change** a **new substance** is formed and it cannot be easily reversed: **burning wood, rusting iron, cooking an egg, baking bread, milk going sour**.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Thinking that sugar disappears when it dissolves.
- Using filtering to separate salt that is dissolved in water: the salt passes through the filter.
- Thinking that all changes can be reversed.
- Confusing melting with dissolving.

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.statement: How can you get salt from sea water?
steps: The salt is dissolved, so a filter cannot remove it.
Heat the water so that it evaporates: the salt is left behind.

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.statement: Is burning a piece of wood a physical or a chemical change? Why?
steps: Burning makes new substances (ash, smoke) and the wood cannot be got back.
So it is a chemical change.
blocks.answer: A chemical change: new substances are formed.

lessons.title: Energy: forms, sources and changes
lessons.programRef: MINEDUB primary school curriculum (English-speaking subsystem), Level III (Class 5) — Elementary Science and Technology; to be checked against the official syllabus
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
reviewNotes: Energy forms listed in a simple way; check the terms used in the official syllabus.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Energy
blocks.md: **Energy** is what makes things happen: it lets us **work, move, heat and light**. It comes in many **forms**: heat, light, sound, electrical, chemical (stored in food, firewood and fuel) and movement. Energy is never made or lost: it is **changed** from one form into another.

blocks.caption: Forms of energy and examples.
blocks.alt: A table with forms of energy: heat, light, sound, electrical, chemical stored in food and fuel, and movement, each with an example.

blocks.title: Sources and changes
blocks.md: **Renewable** sources do not run out: the **Sun**, **wind**, **flowing water** (hydroelectric power from dams) and wood if trees are replanted. **Non-renewable** sources run out one day: **petroleum**, **coal** and **gas**. Energy changes: in a torch, **chemical** energy in the cell becomes **electrical** and then **light** and a little **heat**; our body changes the chemical energy of food into **movement** and **heat**.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Saying that energy is used up: it changes form.
- Thinking that firewood is a never-ending source if forests are not replanted.
- Saying that the Sun is non-renewable.
- Wasting energy by leaving lights and appliances on.

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.statement: Name the energy changes in a bulb that is lit by a cell.
steps: The cell has chemical energy which becomes electrical energy.
The bulb changes it into light and some heat.

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.statement: Is petroleum a renewable source? Give a reason.
steps: Petroleum took millions of years to form.
We use it much faster than nature can make it, so it will run out.
blocks.answer: No: it is non-renewable, because it will run out.

lessons.title: Heat transfer, mirrors and light
lessons.programRef: MINEDUB primary school curriculum (English-speaking subsystem), Level III (Class 5) — Elementary Science and Technology; to be checked against the official syllabus
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Name the three ways in which heat moves.
Say how a mirror reflects light.
Say what happens when white light passes through water drops.
reviewNotes: Light and heat statements are standard; angle values are invented examples.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Heat transfer
blocks.md: **Conduction**: heat passes through **solids**, especially metals (a metal spoon in hot soup). **Convection**: heat moves in **liquids and gases** because warm liquid or air **rises** and cool liquid or air sinks (boiling water, a rising smoke). **Radiation**: heat travels from the **Sun** through empty space. **Insulators** such as wood, plastic, air and wool slow down heat flow.

blocks.caption: How heat moves.
blocks.alt: A table with conduction in solids, convection in liquids and gases, and radiation through space, with examples.

blocks.title: Reflection and colours
blocks.md: A **mirror reflects** light: the angle at which light **hits** the mirror equals the angle at which it **bounces off**. **White light** is a mixture of colours: a **rainbow** forms when sunlight passes through raindrops and splits into the colours red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo and violet.

blocks.caption: Light reflecting from a mirror.
blocks.alt: A flat mirror at the bottom. A ray comes down from the upper left and bounces up to the upper right at the same angle on the other side of the normal line.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Saying that cold flows into a thing: heat flows **out** of hot things.
- Thinking that a woollen jumper makes heat: it keeps in the body's heat.
- Looking at the Sun or reflecting sunlight into someone's eyes.
- Thinking that the rainbow is an object: it is an effect of light and water.

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.statement: Why does a metal spoon get hot at the end when it stands in a hot pot?
steps: Metals conduct heat well.
Heat passes along the spoon from the hot soup to the handle.

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.statement: A ray of light hits a mirror at an angle of 40° to the normal. What is the angle of the reflected ray?
steps: The angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence.
So the reflected ray makes 40° with the normal.

lessons.title: Electricity: series circuits, conductors and safety
lessons.programRef: MINEDUB primary school curriculum (English-speaking subsystem), Level III (Class 5) — Elementary Science and Technology; to be checked against the official syllabus
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Build and describe a series circuit.
Say what happens when more bulbs are added.
Know where electricity comes from and how to be safe.
reviewNotes: Safety rules and experiments must be supervised by a teacher; a parallel circuit is not covered.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Circuits
blocks.md: A **circuit** is a complete loop through which electricity flows. In a **series circuit** the parts (cell, switch, bulbs) are in **one loop**. If one bulb breaks, the loop is broken and **all the bulbs go out**. If you add more bulbs to one cell, each bulb is **dimmer**. A **switch** opens or closes the circuit.

blocks.caption: A series circuit with a cell and two bulbs.
blocks.alt: A single loop of wire with a cell on the left and two bulbs in a row at the top. The note says series circuit: one loop.

blocks.title: Conductors and sources
blocks.md: **Conductors** (copper, iron, aluminium, graphite) let electricity pass; **insulators** (plastic, rubber, glass, dry wood) do not. Wires are copper covered with plastic for safety. Electricity can come from **cells**, from **generators**, from **solar panels** and from **dams** on rivers such as the Sanaga that drive generators.

blocks.title: Safety
blocks.md: **Never** touch bare wires or sockets. **Never** use electrical things with wet hands or near water. Do not pull a plug by its cable. Keep away from fallen cables and **tell an adult**. At school use only **small cells** and a teacher present, never the mains.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Thinking that electricity is 'used up' by a bulb: the energy changes into light and heat, the current goes round.
- Believing that more cells always means a dimmer bulb: more cells make it brighter, more bulbs make each dimmer.
- Using a wet hand to switch on a light.
- Thinking that all metals are safe to touch near power lines.

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.statement: In a series circuit with two bulbs, one bulb breaks. What happens to the other one?
steps: The break stops the flow round the single loop.
The other bulb also goes out.
blocks.answer: It goes out, because the circuit is broken.

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.statement: A circuit with one cell and one bulb has a second bulb added in series. What happens to the brightness?
steps: The same energy from the cell now lights two bulbs.
Each bulb is dimmer.

lessons.title: Forces and simple machines
lessons.programRef: MINEDUB primary school curriculum (English-speaking subsystem), Level III (Class 5) — Elementary Science and Technology; to be checked against the official syllabus
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Say what a force is, and give examples of friction and gravity.
Name the simple machines and their uses.
Say how a lever makes work easier.
reviewNotes: Mass and weight are only mentioned briefly; whether the newton is taught at Class 5 is to be checked.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Forces
blocks.md: A **force** is a **push or a pull**. It can start or stop movement, change speed or direction, or change shape. Forces are measured in **newtons (N)**. **Friction** is a force that **slows** things down where surfaces rub together; rough surfaces have more friction than smooth ones. **Gravity** pulls everything **down** towards the Earth and gives things their **weight**.

blocks.title: Simple machines
blocks.md: A **machine** makes a job easier. **Simple machines** are the **lever** (see-saw, wheelbarrow, scissors, a spade), **pulley** (raising a bucket or a flag), **inclined plane** (a ramp), **wheel and axle** (a bicycle wheel), **screw** and **wedge** (an axe, a knife). They let us use a **smaller force** over a **longer distance**, or change its direction.

blocks.caption: A lever: effort, fulcrum and load.
blocks.alt: A beam resting on a triangular pivot called the fulcrum. A heavy load is on the left and a downward arrow for the effort is on the right.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Thinking that heavier objects always fall faster: without air resistance they fall together.
- Thinking that a machine reduces the total work: it only makes the force smaller or changes its direction.
- Confusing mass (kg) with weight (a force in N).
- Thinking that friction is always bad: without it we could not walk or stop a bicycle.

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.statement: Why do we put oil on a bicycle chain?
steps: Oil makes the surfaces smoother.
So friction is smaller and the chain moves easily.

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.statement: A heavy drum must be put on a lorry 1 m high. Which simple machine helps?
steps: A ramp lets the drum be pushed up gradually.
It is an inclined plane.
